metadata.name: ip
metadata.displayName: ip - Show/manipulate routing, network devices, interfaces
metadata.description: Modern replacement for ifconfig, show and manipulate routing, network devices, interfaces and tunnels

installation.note: ip is part of iproute2 package, pre-installed on modern Ubuntu systems

overview.summary: The ip command is a powerful utility for managing network interfaces, routing tables, and network configuration. It's the modern replacement for ifconfig, route, and arp commands, providing a unified interface for network management.

syntax.description: ip command uses objects (link, addr, route, etc.) and subcommands to manage different aspects of networking.

options.use_case: See detailed statistics like packet counts and errors
Filter output to show only IPv4 or IPv6 addresses

examples.title: Show all network interfaces
examples.description: Display all network interfaces with their IP addresses
examples.output:
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN group default qlen 1000
    link/loopback 00:00:00:00:00:00 brd 00:00:00:00:00:00
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 08:00:27:xx:xx:xx brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 192.168.1.100/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global dynamic eth0
       valid_lft 86399sec preferred_lft 86399sec

elements.meaning: e.g., '1: lo' - loopback interface, '2: eth0' - ethernet interface
UP = interface is active, LOWER_UP = physical link is up
IPv4 address with subnet mask (CIDR notation)
Address scope: host (localhost), global (internet), link (local network)
Lifetime for DHCP addresses (forever for static)

output_explanation.notes: Use 'ip -br addr show' for a more compact view

examples.description: Show interfaces in a compact format

elements.meaning: UP = active, DOWN = inactive, UNKNOWN = loopback
IPv4 and IPv6 addresses assigned to the interface

common_misconceptions.title: ip vs ifconfig
common_misconceptions.misconception: ip and ifconfig do the same thing
common_misconceptions.reality: ip is the modern replacement. ifconfig is deprecated and may not show all information. ip is more powerful and recommended.
common_misconceptions.tip: Use 'ip' instead of 'ifconfig' on modern Linux systems

common_misconceptions.title: Permanent configuration
common_misconceptions.reality: ip commands make temporary changes that are lost on reboot. Use netplan, NetworkManager, or /etc/network/interfaces for permanent configuration.
common_misconceptions.tip: Use ip for temporary testing, use configuration files for permanent changes

common_pitfalls.description: Most ip configuration commands require root privileges
common_pitfalls.solution: Use sudo for configuration commands: sudo ip addr add ...

common_pitfalls.description: Changes made with ip are lost on reboot
common_pitfalls.solution: For permanent changes, use system configuration files (netplan on Ubuntu 18.04+)

common_pitfalls.description: Using incorrect interface name (eth0 vs enp0s3, etc.)
common_pitfalls.solution: First check interface names with 'ip link show' or 'ip -br link show'

best_practices: Use 'ip -br' for more readable output in daily use
Check interface names first with 'ip link show' before configuring
Use 'ip addr show' to verify changes after configuration
For permanent changes, use netplan (Ubuntu 18.04+) or NetworkManager
Use 'ip -s' to see statistics when troubleshooting network issues
performance_tips: Use 'ip -br' for faster parsing in scripts
Use 'ip -j' for JSON output when scripting
Check routing table with 'ip route' to diagnose connectivity issues
Monitor interface statistics with 'ip -s link show' to identify network problems

related_commands.description: ifconfig is the older command that ip replaces. Use ip instead.
After configuring with ip, use ping to test network connectivity
netstat shows active connections, while ip manages interface configuration

additional_notes.note1: On modern Ubuntu systems, use netplan for permanent network configuration instead of ip commands
additional_notes.note2: Interface names have changed in newer systems (enp0s3 instead of eth0) - always check with 'ip link' first
additional_notes.note3: ip supports many subcommands: 'ip link' (interfaces), 'ip addr' (addresses), 'ip route' (routing), 'ip neigh' (ARP table), etc.
